answer.label: Not Mark Twain — a modern paraphrase of Blaise Pascal
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Mark Twain ever wrote or spoke this line; per Quote Investigator, the Twain credit only surfaces posthumously in the 1970s. The thought traces to Blaise Pascal, whose 1657 Lettres Provinciales closes a letter, “I have made this one longer only because I did not have the leisure to make it shorter.” The familiar English one-liner is a much later paraphrase, not Pascal’s exact words and not Twain’s at all.

source.heading: The real source
source.excerpt: Je n’ai fait celle-ci plus longue que parce que je n’ai pas eu le loisir de la faire plus courte.
trail: The earliest known form is Blaise Pascal’s 1657 Lettres Provinciales, whose 16th letter ends with the leisure-to-make-it-shorter remark.
Quote Investigator tracks the idea being re-credited over centuries — to John Locke (1690), Benjamin Franklin (1750), Cicero, Thoreau and others — long before Twain’s name was ever attached.
Per the same investigation, Mark Twain “did not use it”; a version is pinned to him only in a 1975 newspaper piece, decades after his 1910 death.
Pascal’s original text is freely readable via Wikisource and Project Gutenberg.
source.excerptNote: Pascal’s French close to the 16th Provincial Letter (1657) — literally, “I have made this one longer only because I did not have the leisure to make it shorter.” The snappy modern English “I would have written a shorter letter, but I did not have the time” is a paraphrase that later drifted onto Mark Twain.

source.rightsNote: The underlying line comes from Blaise Pascal’s Lettres Provinciales, first published in 1657, with an English translation issued in London in 1658 — both centuries into the public domain. The modern English one-liner is an anonymous paraphrase carrying no separate, protectable authorship.

author.name: Blaise Pascal
author.heading: About Blaise Pascal
author.bio: Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist and religious philosopher, a founder of probability theory and projective geometry. His Lettres Provinciales (1656–57), a series of polemical letters defending Jansenism against the Jesuits, are landmarks of French prose — and the source of the famous apology for a too-long letter. He is also known for the posthumously published Pensées.

misattribution.heading: How Twain got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “famous-name magnet” quote: a witty, universally relatable line that gets reassigned to the era’s favorite wits. It has been pinned on at least a dozen people across four centuries.

items.why: No Twain letter, book, speech or notebook contains this line. Quote Investigator finds Twain “did not use it,” with a version attached to him only in a 1975 newspaper article — 65 years after his death.

items.who: Winston Churchill, Cicero, Benjamin Franklin, John Locke, Goethe, Voltaire
items.why: All appear as later “quotes” of the idea, but the documented chain runs back to Pascal; see the full attribution timeline.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine source is Blaise Pascal’s 1657 Lettres Provinciales — “I did not have the leisure to make it shorter” — not Mark Twain.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The line endures because it captures a real paradox of writing: concision is harder and slower than sprawl. Editing down to the essential takes the time that a first draft skips — so a short, tight letter is often the more expensive one.

Pascal made the point as a graceful apology at the end of a long polemical letter. Over the centuries writers from Franklin to Thoreau restated it, and in the internet age it settled onto Mark Twain, whose reputation for pithy wit makes almost any clever aphorism ‘sound like him.’
context.pull: Concision costs time — which is exactly the joke.
